claims.text: Steels with sufficiently high chromium content resist corrosion in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments primarily through formation of a protective chromium-rich oxide layer.
The chromium-rich oxide layer forms rapidly and continuously regenerates.
The chromium-rich oxide layer blocks ingress of corrosive species.
Controlled pre-oxidation promotes formation of the chromium oxide layer.
Surface chemical inhibitors can inhibit formation of the chromium oxide layer.
The relevant structural mediator is a coherent, nanometer-scale, chromium-rich surface oxide layer.
Surface chromium oxidizes to form a dense, adherent oxide film.
The chromium oxide film acts as a barrier to oxygen and aggressive ions.
Barrier formation limits further oxidation and reduces the overall corrosion rate.
Samples with a uniform chromium oxide passivation layer will have significantly lower corrosion rates than samples in which oxide formation is inhibited.
Samples with a uniform chromium oxide passivation layer will have significantly lower corrosion rates than steels with lower chromium content.
The passivation mechanism requires chromium content above a critical threshold.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate where oxygen and moderate radiation are present.
Insufficient chromium can prevent the proposed passivation mechanism from operating.
Highly reducing atmospheres or very high radiation doses can compromise chromium oxide film formation or stability.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field describes the samples as having known high chromium content, whereas the proposed experiment requires samples with varying chromium contents, including lower-chromium controls.

The baseline places lower-chromium or oxide-inhibited samples under non-aggressive atmospheric conditions, while the intervention and falsification design compare groups in a controlled corrosive environment. This makes the stated baseline inconsistent with the intended controlled comparison and confounds oxide effects with environmental aggressiveness.
